segments.summary: Allard opposed tension-based teaching, fixed reeds, stayed a friend, and Liebman's later book came from two summers of questioning him.

segments.title: On the road with Ten Wheel Drive and the macrobiotic lesson
segments.summary: The band toured East Coast rock festivals; Liebman cooked his own macrobiotic food in Gainesville and learned to go with the flow.

segments.title: Steve Satten, club-date partner
segments.summary: Liebman and Kirchner talk about their friend Steve Satten, his record on Columbia and his label.

segments.title: Horn section quits Ten Wheel Drive; the band Sawbuck
segments.summary: The horns quit over management, formed Sawbuck with Link Chamberlain and Sky Ford, got a Motown deal, and Liebman left when Elvin called.

segments.title: Auditioning for Elvin Jones and joining the band
segments.summary: Gene Perla brought him to a late-night audition at Slugs, followed by the Genesis session at Van Gelder's and an offer from Elvin in Chicago to replace Joe Farrell.

segments.title: An Elvin quartet gig in 1971 and Joe Farrell's flute playing
segments.summary: Kirchner recalls first hearing the band at a Goddard Riverside concert; both praise Joe Farrell's flute and Liebman explains why he stopped playing it.

segments.title: Declining Joe Farrell's Plaza Hotel gig and studio work
segments.summary: Farrell offered him a Plaza double; Liebman declined, closing the door on studio work, and worried about making a living on Elvin's pay.

segments.title: Elvin Jones records: Genesis, Merry-Go-Round and Live at the Lighthouse
segments.summary: They list Elvin's albums with Liebman; Lighthouse captured the post-Coltrane pentatonic language he and Grossman shared.

segments.title: Passing generations of New York saxophonists; Elvin as the heaviest person he knew
segments.summary: He describes the cycle of saxophone favorites and gives a long tribute to Elvin Jones's feel and spiritual weight.

segments.title: Why Elvin's band had no piano or trumpet; length of the tenure
segments.summary: Liebman speculates that Elvin wanted open fullness of sound, and tries to date his time in the band.

segments.title: How he came into Miles Davis's orbit
segments.summary: Through Lenny White, Dave Holland and Grossman, and a Danny's Hideaway afternoon, Miles got to know him; Teo Macero then called him to a session.

segments.title: The On the Corner session and Miles's first 'join my band'
segments.summary: He walked into the huge June 1972 session with no headphones, played soprano on On the Corner, and Miles told him to join his band.

segments.title: Miles's recruitment: Elvin's blessing and the first night at Miles's house
segments.summary: After Miles courted him at the Vanguard, Elvin gave his blessing, and Liebman was taken to Miles's house to hear a Sly Stone track.

segments.title: Miles's offer, the Varitone pickup and the Fillmore debut
segments.summary: Miles offered him $400 a night; he had pickups drilled into his horns, debuted at the Fillmore, then hurried to hear Elvin at the Vanguard the same night.

segments.title: No rehearsals, one book, and Miles's lack of instruction
segments.summary: Miles's band rarely rehearsed, played the same set nightly, and Miles gave almost no direction beyond 'play thirds' and 'finish before you're done'.

segments.title: Drugs, tension and race in Miles's band
segments.summary: He describes Miles's pills and pain, the black-white tension in the band, and Miles taping every night and conducting the music.

segments.title: Finding something to play in Miles's open-ended music
segments.summary: The repetitive vamps felt unchallenging and gave no interaction, yet Miles told stories in them; Liebman still draws on the lesson.

segments.title: Miles and Liebman's leg
segments.summary: Miles respected how Liebman got around with his polio leg and asked how he did it as his own body failed.

segments.title: How the music was built: bass lines, Michael Henderson and Pete Cosey
segments.summary: Miles's pieces began from bass lines and short melodies; they discuss Michael Henderson, Reggie Lucas and Pete Cosey's blues and AACM background.

segments.title: Al Foster and Miles as director who heard what he wanted in you
segments.summary: Al Foster came from bebop; Liebman says Miles's sidemen played in ways they never repeated, because Miles heard and cast them like a film director.

segments.title: Electric bands as Miles's Gil Evans color
segments.summary: Kirchner suggests Miles's electric bands recreated Gil Evans's orchestral color, and Liebman agrees that color serves the story like harmony.

segments.title: Carnegie Hall, Dark Magus and Azar Lawrence
segments.summary: At the Carnegie Hall concert recorded as Dark Magus, Mtume brought in Azar Lawrence, which angered Liebman; Miles arrived late.

segments.title: Leaving Miles in Brazil to lead his own band
segments.summary: He left because he had Lookout Farm and a band in waiting; Miles asked about his plans and Liebman gave notice in Brazil.

segments.title: He Loved Him Madly, the last Miles recording
segments.summary: After Duke Ellington died, Miles recorded the 27-minute He Loved Him Madly, with Liebman on flute, a month after he left; they check the discography.

segments.title: Why Miles played organ
segments.summary: Miles took over the keyboard after his organists left, using triads and clusters for color; Liebman recalls playing piano for him in Japan.

segments.title: Open Sky with Bob Moses and Eugene Gregan of Lookout Farm
segments.summary: His free trio Open Sky with Moses came out of the loft; he also describes painter Eugene Gregan, the namesake of Lookout Farm.

segments.title: Naming Lookout Farm and recording for ECM
segments.summary: Manfred Eicher approached him at Berlin festivals and recorded the Lookout Farm band with Beirach, Tusa and Jeff Williams in New York.

segments.title: Sidemen as indentured servants and the end of the apprenticeship system
segments.summary: Coming out of Miles earned him a shot at leading; he reflects that leaders owned their sidemen and the system died when steady work did.

segments.title: The book of Lookout Farm music with Chuck Berg
segments.summary: The band's co-op process, nightly tape listening and the book on composition and performance recorded by Chuck Berg for A&M.

segments.chapter: A&M, Indian music and the California fusion attempt
segments.title: A&M and Horizon: John Snyder's blank check and a promotion tour
segments.summary: Signed to A&M's jazz label Horizon, he enjoyed an expense account and a limo-filled promotion tour; Snyder had called him as his second choice.

segments.chapter: A&M, Indian music and the California fusion attempt
segments.title: Sweet Hands and the Indian music influence of Badal Roy
segments.summary: Badal Roy led Liebman into Indian music, shaping the album Sweet Hands, which he describes with its meaning.

segments.chapter: A&M, Indian music and the California fusion attempt
segments.title: Forgotten Fantasies, the duo record with Richie Beirach
segments.summary: Snyder let him record a duo album at Electric Ladyland to capture his harmonic language with Beirach.

segments.chapter: A&M, Indian music and the California fusion attempt
segments.title: Ellis-Liebman band: trying to merge Coltrane and James Brown
segments.summary: Wanting to cash in on fusion, he moved to San Francisco with Pee Wee Ellis and a backer, spent about $60,000, and the project folded.

segments.chapter: A&M, Indian music and the California fusion attempt
segments.title: San Francisco jazz gigs with Eddie Henderson and lessons learned
segments.summary: After the project failed he worked a nearly empty club with Eddie Henderson and Julian Priester until Chick Corea called.

segments.chapter: A&M, Indian music and the California fusion attempt
segments.title: The San Francisco band members and why fusion halfway failed
segments.summary: He names the band (Jimmy Strassburg, Tony Saunders, Chris Hayes) and explains that the band lacked an identity, neither jazz nor commercial enough.

segments.chapter: A&M, Indian music and the California fusion attempt
segments.title: Burned out on New York at thirty
segments.summary: He left New York because his life was out of control from drugs and women after six years of Miles, Elvin and Lookout Farm.

segments.chapter: A&M, Indian music and the California fusion attempt
segments.title: Rapson's in Port Chester with Link Chamberlain and Enrico Rava
segments.summary: Kirchner recalls the Rapson's gig with Chamberlain, Strassburg, Vicari and Rava; Liebman describes Chamberlain and the border-town bar.

segments.chapter: Beirach, harmony and the dotted feel
segments.title: End of the first session; start of the second day
segments.summary: The engineer calls time, the session ends, and the next day Kirchner asks Liebman to explain his painter friend Eugene Gregan.

segments.chapter: Beirach, harmony and the dotted feel
segments.title: Eugene Gregan and learning from other artists' process
segments.summary: Liebman describes the painter's work and says reading artists' accounts of their process, like van Gogh's letters, enlarges a musician's view; they note jazz musicians who painted.

segments.chapter: Beirach, harmony and the dotted feel
segments.title: Richie Beirach: same neighborhood, quick wit, escaping influences
segments.summary: Liebman describes his lifelong partnership with Beirach, their shared Brooklyn roots and their search to escape the influence of the great pianists.

segments.chapter: Beirach, harmony and the dotted feel
segments.title: Beirach's 20th-century harmony and the partnership over the years
segments.summary: Beirach dug deeply into Schoenberg and Bartok voicings; Liebman learned from him, and traces their work together through Lookout Farm, Quest and the present.

segments.chapter: Beirach, harmony and the dotted feel
segments.title: Beirach's life now: Leipzig professorship, health and plans to record Miles repertoire
segments.summary: Liebman updates Beirach's personal situation and LeeAnn Ledgerwood, and describes the upcoming Birdland gig and Miles-repertoire recording.

segments.chapter: Beirach, harmony and the dotted feel
segments.title: Beirach as source of A Chromatic Approach, and their fifteen-year split
segments.summary: Liebman credits Beirach as the main source of the Chromatic Approach book and recounts the break after Quest and their reunion in 2005.

segments.chapter: Beirach, harmony and the dotted feel
segments.title: What A Chromatic Approach to Jazz Harmony and Melody teaches
segments.summary: He explains the book as a workbook for going outside the key, built on facility with changes, and how he teaches it at Manhattan.

segments.chapter: Beirach, harmony and the dotted feel
segments.title: The even-eighth feel versus the dotted bebop feel
segments.summary: Kirchner asks about even-eighth-note playing; Liebman credits Coltrane and explains why fusion needs it and how he drills students on both feels.

segments.chapter: Beirach, harmony and the dotted feel
segments.title: Lineage of the even feel: Pres, Dexter, Bix and cultural roots
segments.summary: They trace Coltrane's evenness back through Dexter Gordon and Lester Young to Bix, and Liebman speculates about heredity and geography.

segments.title: Not being a music major: the value of a college education
segments.summary: Kirchner and Liebman compare English and history degrees to music study; Liebman says his degree shaped his thinking though he felt late to the New York scene.

segments.title: No jazz programs then: the advantage of finding your own way
segments.summary: He envies students' complete education but says trial and error forced his generation to find individuality.

segments.title: Why young saxophonists sound alike
segments.summary: Liebman argues individuality is always rare, and today's schooling teaches to the mean, so many talented young players sound the same.

segments.title: Refusing to judge competitions and contests
segments.summary: He refuses prizes in music, arguing jazz is communal, and says awards send a bad message to young players.

segments.title: Chick Corea's call and the 1977 string-and-brass world tour
segments.summary: In Houston he got Chick's call to replace Joe Farrell on a world tour with strings and brass, which taught him about composition and got him back to New York.

segments.title: Scientology and the blow-up with Chick Corea
segments.summary: Nightly arguments about Scientology, a joint and a romance ended with Corea telling him he never wanted to see him again; Liebman still rates Corea a great musician.

segments.chapter: The Scofield-Hino quintet and return to New York
segments.title: Ending Lookout Farm and wanting guitar and more composed form
segments.summary: He explains letting Beirach go solo and wanting guitar and written form after the Chick tour.

segments.chapter: The Scofield-Hino quintet and return to New York
segments.title: Forming the quintet with Scofield and Hino; Moses quits, Adam Nussbaum steps in
segments.summary: He assembled John Scofield, Terumasa Hino and Mike Formanek, but Bob Moses quit before the Sweet Basil opening and Adam Nussbaum replaced him.

segments.chapter: The Scofield-Hino quintet and return to New York
segments.title: The Timeless records, Scofield and Hino, and moving back to New York
segments.summary: The quintet made Doin' It Again and If They Only Knew over about three years; Liebman describes Scofield and Hino and his return to New York life and a short marriage.

segments.title: Mid-life restlessness and the old wish to be a surgeon
segments.summary: Back in New York he felt his bandleading was going nowhere at 35, wanted to do something for the world, and recalled his childhood wish to be a doctor.

segments.title: Law school acceptances and applying to aid agencies
segments.summary: He took the LSATs and got into law school, sat in a criminal trial, declined, then tried Save the Children without luck.

segments.title: Breaking his leg, divorce, and the first Jamey Aebersold clinic
segments.summary: A broken leg, hepatitis and divorce in 1981 added to his crisis; he recalls his first jazz-education clinic with Aebersold, Baker and Coker.

segments.title: Jerry Coker, Aebersold and deciding to teach
segments.summary: He recalls Coker's ear and Aebersold's clinics, and concludes teaching would give him a living and meaning.

segments.title: Teaching as purpose: Banff, East Stroudsburg and not being Coltrane
segments.summary: Clinics led to Banff and East Stroudsburg; he says that if you are not a Mozart or Coltrane you should find work of value beyond your own art.

segments.title: Accepting he is not Coltrane; teaching as a mission
segments.summary: Coping with Coltrane's shadow, Liebman found meaning in turning kids onto jazz, with Phil Woods's remark about horns and guns.

segments.title: Jazz as a model of improvisation and democratic values
segments.summary: Kirchner cites Toffler on improvisers; Liebman says jazz embodies positive democratic values that no autocratic culture would produce.

segments.chapter: The IASJ and a career in education
segments.title: Founding the International Association of Schools of Jazz, 1989
segments.summary: Frustrated that European jazz students did not know each other's countries, he wrote to teachers worldwide and held a 1989 Stuttgart meeting that started the IASJ with Walter Turkenburg.

segments.chapter: The IASJ and a career in education
segments.title: Leading the IASJ: Berklee meeting, etiquette and psychology
segments.summary: Kirchner recalls the 2001 Berklee meeting; Liebman says running the organization taught him sensitivity across cultures.

segments.chapter: The IASJ and a career in education
segments.title: Student-to-student versus IAJE, and Turkenburg as executive director
segments.summary: He explains how the IASJ differs from the IAJE, how IAJE came to give $1500 a year, and how Turkenburg set up the first meeting at The Hague.

segments.chapter: The IASJ and a career in education
segments.title: IASJ membership and European funding cuts
segments.summary: The IASJ has about 40 countries but European budget cuts are costing members and may affect a meeting in Ireland.

segments.chapter: The IASJ and a career in education
segments.title: Working mostly in Europe and the missing middle tier in America
segments.summary: Eighty to ninety percent of his work is in Europe; he explains American jazz income as A-level or nothing and cites Joe Henderson's revival.

segments.chapter: The IASJ and a career in education
segments.title: Education as his real contribution and why he accepts it
segments.summary: He says he is a hustler of modest commercial success and believes his teaching and books are his lasting effect, reflected in the NEA award.

segments.chapter: The IASJ and a career in education
segments.title: Michael Brecker's down period and balancing playing with teaching
segments.summary: Using Brecker as an example of commercial success, he says education was the way things were meant to be and that his teaching and playing credit each other.

segments.chapter: The IASJ and a career in education
segments.title: Why he does his own bookings
segments.summary: Nobody else can book his work as he does, and foreign promoters want to deal with Dave directly.

segments.title: Starting Quest: playing jazz after fusion with Beirach
segments.summary: He and Beirach resumed in the early 1980s to play jazz modelled on the Miles and Coltrane quartets of the 1960s.

segments.title: Quest's rhythm section, success and breakup
segments.summary: With Al Foster and George Mraz, then Billy Hart and Ron McClure, Quest was a celebrated 1980s band until drug and road problems ended it.

segments.title: Reuniting with Beirach in 2005
segments.summary: After fifteen years apart a friend's Swiss birthday party led to a duo and then to a reunion of Quest in 2005.

segments.title: The Vic Juris band and unsung guitarists
segments.summary: Liebman praises his working band with Vic Juris and Tony Marino and laments the neglect of Abercrombie and the Goodrick lineage of guitarists.

segments.title: Manfred Eicher and the Drum Ode blow-up
segments.summary: Liebman discusses Abercrombie's long ECM tenure and how he broke with Eicher at the smoky eight-drummer Drum Ode session.

segments.title: Giving up tenor for soprano: escaping Coltrane and the recipe
segments.summary: Around 1980-81 he stopped playing tenor to escape Coltrane and the formula of tenor for blowing, soprano for fusion, flute for ethnic.

segments.title: Doubling too thin; why soprano felt natural
segments.summary: Spread across three horns he was not mastering any; soprano felt physically natural and carried Miles's trumpet ideas.

segments.title: Dropping flute, copyists of his tenor language, and returning to tenor
segments.summary: Imitators of his tenor language bothered him; soprano improved within two years, and he picked tenor up again around age fifty.

segments.title: Wayne Shorter's articulation enters his tenor playing
segments.summary: After returning to tenor, Liebman heard Shorter's speech-like articulation appearing in his own playing.

segments.title: Playing a Coltrane tribute with Wayne Shorter on crutches
segments.summary: Breaking his leg in California he still flew to Japan for the best-paying gig of his life, a Coltrane tribute festival with Shorter, DeJohnette, Gomez and Beirach.

segments.title: Standing beside Shorter: stillness, embouchure and ear
segments.summary: Next to Shorter he marvelled at his perfectly still classical embouchure and quick ear.

segments.title: The Japan festival night: choosing tunes and Naima before 20,000
segments.summary: He recalls the hotel-lobby tune discussion, Shorter's promise to float like Eric Dolphy, the long wait, and playing Naima with Beirach before 20,000.

segments.title: Sopranino, G soprano and soprano pitfalls
segments.summary: Kirchner and Liebman compare sopranino and lower-pitched sopranos and mouthpieces, with a joke about the altissimo.

segments.title: His self-portrait book and the planned biography with Lewis Porter
segments.summary: The book explains how he became who he is, and he describes the upcoming biographical book with Lewis Porter.

segments.title: Why people hate the soprano saxophone
segments.summary: Liebman agrees the soprano is high and annoying, hard to play in tune, and even Max Gordon disliked it.

segments.title: Soprano's difficulty, doubling, and the advantage of its register
segments.summary: Most soprano players play it badly because of doubling; Liebman says its register matches the piano and cuts through.

segments.title: Curved sopranos and Jan Garbarek's sound
segments.summary: Both dislike curved sopranos, though Liebman admires Garbarek, whose stark declarative style fits his sound.

segments.title: Straight horns, airstream and Freddie Hubbard's time feel
segments.summary: He says a straight horn's immediate airstream let him borrow trumpet articulation, and they discuss Freddie Hubbard's solo on Birdlike.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: Letting Phil Markowitz go to feature Vic Juris
segments.summary: He dropped the keyboardist to cut costs and give guitarist Vic Juris more responsibility; drummer Jamey Haddad left for Paul Simon.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: Rock stars hiring jazz sidemen: staying on his side of the tracks
segments.summary: Liebman resents pop stars like Paul Simon and Sting hiring jazz musicians for eight bars and takes lessons from them, while Kirchner recalls the 'where do I go to sell out' line.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: How he became a big-band leader
segments.summary: Through school clinics, student arrangers wrote charts of his tunes, and he fronts the band on soprano.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: McNeely's big-band arrangements and why he disliked sections
segments.summary: The Quest for Freedom record with the Hessian Radio band and Jim McNeely's writing; Liebman says he could never sit in a section.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: Gunnar Mossblad, his aide-de-camp
segments.summary: A former student, Mossblad arranges and organizes for Liebman, including the big-band Meditations arrangement.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: 1997 Live by the Sea concert that led to the Saxophone Summit
segments.summary: A 30-year Coltrane tribute at which Garzone replaced the injured Lovano, with Brecker, set up the idea of the Saxophone Summit.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: Persuading Michael Brecker and choosing the rhythm section
segments.summary: He told Brecker that they owed Coltrane a live tribute, and insisted on a rhythm section including Billy Hart.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: After Michael's death: keeping the Saxophone Summit going with Ravi Coltrane
segments.summary: Brecker died on the night of IAJE; Liebman and Lovano chose Ravi Coltrane after trying other saxophonists on three gigs.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: Performing Coltrane's Meditations; Caris's transcription
segments.summary: The band played Meditations every night on a November tour using Caris Visentin's transcription, and Liebman wrote an analysis of the piece.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: McCoy Tyner's silence and the secret-society habit of older musicians
segments.summary: McCoy would reveal nothing about how Meditations was made, which Liebman links to old musicians who did not teach, with Dizzy as an exception.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: Planning a free Saxophone Summit record with originals
segments.summary: He asked each member to bring pieces for a looser album, with no Coltrane or standards, and describes a recent session with Cecil McBee and Billy Hart.

segments.chapter: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
segments.title: Telarc fees and splitting pay evenly with Michael Brecker
segments.summary: Telarc paid for the records; Liebman insisted sidemen be paid fairly and the leaders' share split three ways, with Brecker agreeing.

segments.title: First trip to Europe and Lars Werner's record in Stockholm
segments.summary: At 20 he travelled with $1,000, met Dave Holland in London, and learned of Coltrane's death while recording his first record with Lars Werner in Sweden.

segments.title: Terumasa Hino's Journey to Air session
segments.summary: Kirchner reads the personnel of Hino's 1970 New York session, which Liebman likens to Ascension.

segments.title: Dave Holland and Chick Corea in the West 19th Street building; meeting McLaughlin
segments.summary: He got Holland and then Corea into his loft building and befriended McLaughlin before playing on his record.

segments.title: John McLaughlin's My Goal's Beyond and dating the Elvin Jones tenure
segments.summary: They go through personnel of My Goal's Beyond and use dates to place Genesis and the start of his time with Elvin.

segments.title: Open Sky, PM Records and Petter Wettre's Lighthouse solo transcriptions
segments.summary: The WBAI Open Sky concert on Gene Perla's PM label, and a Norwegian student's book transcribing every Liebman and Grossman solo from Lighthouse.

segments.title: Steve Grossman's rivalry, friendship and puzzling style change
segments.summary: Liebman recounts the early rivalry with Grossman, their reconciliation over Coltrane, and cannot explain why he later became a hard-bop player.

segments.title: Mr. Jones date with Elvin Jones
segments.summary: Liebman recalls the many percussionists on the July 1972 Mr. Jones sessions and is unsure which tunes were recorded that day.

segments.title: First Visit in Japan, Abbey Lincoln, Spirit in the Sky and Drum Ode dates
segments.summary: They run through his first Japan record date, the Abbey Lincoln session, Open Sky overdubs, Drum Ode's date, a Bob Moses big-band record, and trumpeter Mike Lawrence.

segments.title: Recording with Indian musicians in Bombay on the State Department tour
segments.summary: On the India tour he and Beirach recorded Passing Dreams with four Indian musicians in a midnight TV studio, a highlight of his life.

segments.title: Live Lookout Farm at Keystone Korner and The Last Call
segments.summary: A&M let him record live at Keystone Korner; The Last Call featured his young San Francisco group and was released only around 1981.

segments.title: Link Chamberlain's record and Kikuchi's Japanese Miles-inspired date
segments.summary: They recall playing on Link Chamberlain's leader date and Masabumi Kikuchi's On the Corner-style record, part of his run of Japanese dates.

segments.title: Pendulum at the Vanguard and praise for Randy Brecker
segments.summary: Pendulum was the beginning of Quest; Liebman calls Randy Brecker his favorite trumpeter and discusses his career choices.

segments.title: The Australian quartet with Mike Nock and a commercial fusion date
segments.summary: A record made after a Jamey clinic in Australia with Mike Nock, plus a commercial fusion session for Japanese keyboardist Sato.

segments.title: Three records with John McNeil and meeting Billy Hart
segments.summary: They go through three Steeplechase dates with John McNeil, through which Liebman met drummer Billy Hart.

segments.title: Bob Moses's Family and Swallow's Home on ECM
segments.summary: Two records from the same band period; Home was Swallow's ECM album, his first time seeing Manfred Eicher after the Drum Ode blow-up.

segments.title: Dedications for string quartet and the start of soprano-only records
segments.summary: After Chick's string tour he studied quartet literature and wrote Dedications, his first soprano-only album and start of his relationship with CMP.

segments.title: Hino's Day Dreams and Hino leaving the quintet
segments.summary: On Hino's big-budget Japanese session, Liebman recalls Hino leaving his quintet without being able to say so.

segments.title: Memories, Dreams and Reflections: his solo record and writing programmatic tunes
segments.summary: His solo multi-instrument record on Gene Perla's label drew on Jung, Satie and Borges; he explains most of his tunes are about a person, place or incident.

segments.title: Lieb Up Close, Moses's Gramavision date and Jill McManus
segments.summary: Quick comments on a Steve Satten swing date, a Bob Moses Gramavision record and Jill McManus's Hopi-based album.

segments.title: Jukkis Uotila's Introspection and Don Thompson's date
segments.summary: They recall a Finnish record date with Frisell, Formanek and Samuels, and Don Thompson's Canadian date with Claude Ranger.

segments.title: Teo Macero's chaotic sessions and his role behind Miles
segments.summary: Liebman describes Macero's disorganized dates and argues Miles Davis's records owe their shape to Macero's editing.

segments.title: The Loneliness of a Long Distance Runner, his composed soprano record
segments.summary: Inspired by the idea of the artist as a marathon runner, he wrote out a heavily composed multi-soprano album around the time he met Caris.

segments.title: Moses's Story of Moses and Homage to John Coltrane for Owl
segments.summary: He was 'the burning bush' on a Moses record; a Paris Meditations concert led Owl Records to commission his Coltrane tribute.

segments.title: Tom Harrell's Sail Away and European guest-artist dates
segments.summary: He recalls Harrell's record and says guest dates in Europe such as one with Franco D'Andrea revived his career.

segments.title: Timeline: three-horn writing in the style of Booker Little
segments.summary: He explains Timeline as a three- and four-horn album modeled on Booker Little's records, with Conrad Herwig and Bob Mintzer.

segments.title: Launeddas in Sardinia with Paolo Fresu; Ed Sarath's date
segments.summary: He recorded in Sardinia with the last master of the 3,000-year-old launeddas pipes, and mentions meeting Billy Hart and Cecil McBee as a team on Ed Sarath's record.

segments.title: Playing a church duo with Steve Lacy and the solo record The Tree
segments.summary: Unexpectedly asked to play solo at a Florence church concert with Lacy, he impressed Lacy and then recorded his solo soprano album The Tree.

segments.title: Classique for winds and strings
segments.summary: He calls his composed record for saxophone, woodwind and string quartets one of his favorites.

segments.title: Motohiko Hino's date and New Year's gigs in Japan
segments.summary: They remember drummer Toko Hino, Joe Henderson in Japan, and Liebman's New Year's concerts with Japanese musicians who played bridge all night.

segments.title: Aydin Esen, the unknown genius pianist
segments.summary: Liebman praises Turkish pianist Esen and recalls a disorganized Columbia date with Dave Holland and Peter Erskine.

segments.title: Sax Legends and Steve Coleman's master class
segments.summary: On a Japanese saxophone-legends record he heard Steve Coleman, who later gave the best presentation ever at Liebman's master class.

segments.title: Jarmo Savolainen's True Image and Dave Panichi's date
segments.summary: They recall Finnish pianist Jarmo Savolainen from IASJ meetings and his sad death, and a Dave Panichi album.

segments.title: Meditations on Arkadia and a difficult producer
segments.summary: His first Meditations record came out through Arkadia's producer, who proved a legal headache though a good producer.

segments.title: Jens Winther's piece from the IASJ Baltic cruise of 1996
segments.summary: The IASJ toured ten Baltic countries by boat, and the piece Winther wrote was rehearsed aboard for the Rhythmic Conservatory opening.

segments.title: Vic Juris's Alec Wilder record; Kirchner's afternoon with Wilder
segments.summary: Kirchner tells of meeting Alec Wilder in Rochester; Liebman has only recorded his music.

segments.title: Whether to reharmonize standards: Alec Wilder's objection
segments.summary: They share stories of Wilder's anger at altered tunes, and Liebman teaches both sides of the reharmonization question; they praise Wilder's book American Popular Song and James T. Maher's role in it.

segments.title: Rolf Kuhn's record and the Finnish Hunters and Gatherers
segments.summary: Quick comments on clarinetist Rolf Kuhn's date and on a Finnish record with Jukkis Uotila, Jarmo Savolainen and bassist Anders Jormin.

segments.title: The Puccini record: discovering opera in Lisbon and reharmonizing arias
segments.summary: Stuck watching a Domingo Tosca video in Lisbon, he later studied Puccini scores and reharmonized a dozen tunes for his Puccini album.

segments.title: Florian Ross's live record
segments.summary: Liebman recalls a live date with the young German pianist-composer Florian Ross, whom Kirchner thinks underrated.

segments.title: Banff recording with John Stowell and Don Thompson
segments.summary: At Banff's 25th anniversary he played three standards on a late-night date with guitarist John Stowell, whom both praise.

segments.title: Monk trio without chords, and the Far North group
segments.summary: A Monk album with Eddie Gomez and Adam Nussbaum, and records with the Scandinavian group Far North, who taught him rubato.

segments.title: Duos with Marc Copland, Beirach and Markowitz
segments.summary: Liebman describes his duo albums with Copland and calls Copland, Beirach and Markowitz three elite pianists.

segments.title: Solo records: Colors and the Willisau concert
segments.summary: His one solo concert came after the Colors tenor record, and he says Steve Lacy's solo concentration is beyond him.

segments.title: Dave Kane, Bobby Avey's Vienna Dialogues and recent records
segments.summary: They go through two Dave Kane dates and a classical-based duo with young pianist Bobby Avey as the discography nears its end.

segments.title: Miles from India, Nomads, Saxophone Summit and Manhattan School orchestra dates
segments.summary: Brief comments on Bob Belden's project, the Michael Stephans duo, the Saxophone Summit albums and the Miles Ahead and Sketches of Spain orchestra concerts.

segments.title: The last discography entry and being the last three-records-a-year musician
segments.summary: Kirchner reaches 2010; Liebman jokes that he is the last dinosaur recording three records a year and says self-production lacks a label's help.

segments.title: Closing thanks and the NEA award
segments.summary: Liebman thanks Kirchner and says he is honored to be on the same shelf as his idols among Jazz Masters.
